metaData.originalTitle: I Spent May Evaluating Different Engines for OCR
metaData.title: I Spent May Evaluating Different Engines for OCR
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article presents a practical benchmark of 14 OCR engines against 93 documents of varying difficulty, concluding that OCR is a routing problem with no single best engine.
metaData.summary: The author conducted a hands-on experiment to evaluate 14 different OCR engines—ranging from classical open-source tools like Tesseract to modern specialized models and general-purpose vision-language models—against a diverse set of 93 documents. The documents spanned easy (clean invoices), medium (bank statements, tax forms), and hard (handwritten notes, legacy reports, charts) categories. Key metrics included Coverage (how much ground truth text was captured), Precision/Recall, and latency. The results showed that Gemini Flash 3.1 Lite was the best all-rounder for mixed production documents, Tesseract remains unbeatable for clean high-volume print, and Mistral OCR offers a cost-effective option for structured table extraction. The author emphasizes that there is no universal best engine; OCR is a routing problem where document type, cost, structure needs, and failure tolerance dictate the optimal choice. The article also discusses cost scaling, failure modes of different engines, and caveats about benchmark limitations.

mainPoints.point: There is no single best OCR engine; OCR is a routing problem.
mainPoints.explanation: The optimal engine depends on document type, cost constraints, need for structure, and failure tolerance. A routing strategy that classifies documents and selects the appropriate engine is more effective than using one engine for all.

mainPoints.point: For clean, high-volume print documents, Tesseract is still the best choice due to being free and fast.
mainPoints.explanation: Tesseract outperformed many modern engines on easy documents like clean invoices and receipts, while being orders of magnitude faster and cheaper.

mainPoints.point: Gemini Flash 3.1 Lite was the best all-rounder for mixed production documents.
mainPoints.explanation: It performed consistently well across all difficulty levels, including hard documents like handwritten notes and forms, making it a strong default for heterogeneous document streams.

mainPoints.point: Specialized OCR models have sharp boundaries and fail outside their training distribution.
mainPoints.explanation: Models like PaddleOCR and DeepSeek-OCR performed well on certain document types but exhibited catastrophic failures (e.g., repetition loops, empty outputs) on unfamiliar documents, making them risky for general use without escalation.

mainPoints.point: Do not pay for expensive structured OCR when the document does not need it.
mainPoints.explanation: Using AWS Textract Structured for all documents incurs significant cost ($6.5k per 100k pages) with little text accuracy gain over cheaper alternatives. Classifying documents and routing based on structure needs can drastically reduce costs.

keyQuotes: There is no single best OCR engine. OCR is a routing problem.
Do not pay for expensive structured OCR when the document does not need it.
Benchmarks are useful for discovery, but they will not tell you what works on your documents.
The specialist models... have sharp boundaries. This is where the general models will win.

relatedArticles.title: Dreaming: Better memory for a more helpful ChatGPT
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI announces a major upgrade to ChatGPT's memory system, using a more scalable 'dreaming' architecture that automatically synthesizes memories from chat history to improve freshness, continuity, and relevance.

relatedArticles.title: Embeddings Aren’t Magic: The Predictable Failure Modes of RAG Retrieval
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically debunks the magic of embeddings in RAG systems, demonstrating through reproducible experiments that embeddings excel at public vocabulary tasks but predictably fail on enterprise-specific terms, negation, magnitudes, and answer relevance, advocating for upstream filtering over stronger models.

relatedArticles.title: Andrej Karpathy on Code Agents， AutoResearch， and the Loopy Era of AI
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Andrej Karpathy explores the paradigm shift from manual programming to agent orchestration, the automation of AI research, and the profound implications for software engineering and education.

relatedArticles.title: A harness for every task: dynamic workflows in Claude Code  | Claude
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Claude Code's dynamic workflows let Claude write custom agentic harnesses on the fly, enabling it to tackle complex, multi-step tasks that a single context window cannot handle reliably.

relatedArticles.title: Building an Evaluation Harness for Production AI Agents: A 12-Metric Framework From 100+ Deployments
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article presents a comprehensive 12-metric evaluation framework for production AI agents, distilled from over 100 enterprise deployments, covering retrieval, generation, agent behavior, and production health.

relatedArticles.title: Introducing GPT-5.5
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI introduces GPT-5.5, a new category of AI that acts as an autonomous agent capable of planning, reasoning, and executing complex multi-step tasks across different applications.

relatedArticles.title: Stop Treating AI Memory Like a Search Problem
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article critiques the conventional 'store-and-retrieve' approach to AI memory, proposing a lifecycle-based system with decay, contradiction detection, confidence scoring, compression, and expiry to manage memory like a human brain rather than a static archive.

relatedArticles.title: Your ReAct Agent Is Wasting 90% of Its Retries — Here’s How to Stop It
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article identifies a critical architectural flaw in ReAct-style LLM agents where hallucinated tool names waste the majority of retry budgets, and proposes three structural fixes—error taxonomy, per-tool circuit breakers, and deterministic tool routing—to eliminate this waste and improve production reliability.

relatedArticles.title: Hybrid Search and Re-Ranking in Production RAG
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article presents a production-grade approach to improving RAG retrieval quality by combining hybrid search (BM25 + dense vectors) with cross-encoder re-ranking and metadata filtering, supported by real-world evaluation metrics.
